In April 2015, the Advertising Standards Authority upheld complaints about misleading claims made by Google in a television commercial that portrayed the internet as a place of greater freedom and where users can say, do and see anything they want. The commercial also stated that online was cheaper and easier to use than newspapers. The truth is that for many communities, offline media, newspapers in particular, provide an important forum for information dissemination and political and social engagement – and they are not the only ones. The newspaper landscape is in a state of flux. New media can be used in such a way that it is much more interactive and accessible than a paper newspaper, but it does not automatically ensure these goals. Online media did not start as a completely new media, but rather built on the groundwork laid by print media. It is, therefore, essential that the government continues to support print media and its efforts to develop online platforms. For example, the promotion of free Wi-Fi in local communities can give access to online media – but this does not necessarily mean that everyone will want to use it. Without this support, print media will continue to suffer and the problem will only get worse. The Broadcasting Act 1990 (UK) states that the government is responsible for the strategic development of the news media “with a view to achieving a broadcasting service which is both comprehensive and impartial” and to “foster the provision of a diverse and plural media”. However, it is not always clear how this is achieved. In 2011, the Department of Culture Media and Sport produced a report on how the BBC might be reformed, but this report was criticised for not mentioning print media and its specific challenges. In the heat of the moment, this was widely perceived as a two-minute hate response by a senior church leader, who opposed the embryonic stem cell research on religious grounds. I don't want to enter the interesting public debate on whether the use of human embryonic stem cells is or is not morally acceptable. That is not my specialty and I don't have the expertise or training to assess the scientific and moral complexities of this issue. I do, however, have some reflections on how the church can best present its moral arguments in public without becoming a media sensation. The church has a duty to advise potential voters on moral and ethical issues. It is also one of the few institutions in our society that has the resources, the credibility and the moral legitimacy to explore and articulate deep moral and ethical principles. The ramifications of the public statements of Cardinal Pell, the Pope and even the Vatican Secretary of State were underscored by the powerful impact of their comments on the stem cell research in the world's most secular parliament, the parliament of France. Cardinal Pell was not alone in holding the view that a properly informed conscience clause was a necessity, because it is a matter of public morality, rather than a private choice. In fact, an Inquiry into Ethical and Moral Issues in Stem Cell Research, and the policy statement of the Australian & New Zealand Society for Stem Cell Research, state that the use of embryonic stem cells in research can never be morally justified. This is not to say that the church is not subject to error, but it is a much more reliable source of moral and ethical guidance than many of the sources that are routinely given much more credibility in the public arena. "A significant percentage of our residents, especially in southern Ohio, are dependent on international medical graduates to fill gaps in their communities," she said. J-1 visas, which the ban suspends for people from seven predominantly Muslim countries — Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen — are given to people who come to the U.S. for medical training. Doctors who receive J-1 visas must return to their home countries for two years before they can return to the U.S., but medically under-served areas are exempt from that rule. The Trump administration has made exceptions for J-1 visa holders training in cancer and organ transplant centers, but not for primary care training. Trump spokesman Raj Shah said the ban would help protect Americans from terrorism. "The president is very committed to making sure that we have a very, very rigorous process for anybody who enters this country," he said. Our policy must be based on the assumption that significant portions of Iran’s regime will not keep their word to the United States. To suggest that the United States can assume good faith from the outset is to invite disaster.
That is why I am deeply troubled by the administration’s proposal that sanctions be unfrozen at a specific point in time, regardless of Iran’s behavior. If the administration wants to reassure the Iranian regime that sanctions will be unfrozen, it is in danger of undermining the inspections needed to ensure that Iran follows through on its commitments. If the administration wants to make sure that sanctions can be reimposed if Iran fails to follow through, it is in danger of undermining the Iranian regime’s confidence that sanctions will be unfrozen at all. It is nearly impossible, in other words, to have it both ways.
Therefore, I urge you to propose a sanctions relief mechanism that is based on the requirements of the deal, not a specific date. That way, sanctions will not be frozen at a particular moment, and they will remain available if the Iranian regime fails to live up to its commitments. The administration’s proposal, on the other hand, would likely set a date on which sanctions will be unfrozen and effectively remove sanctions from the leverage needed to keep Iran in line.
As the negotiations continue, you may find that the Iranian regime is unwilling to agree to an alternate sanctions relief mechanism. In that case, I urge you to make it clear that sanctions relief will be contingent on Iran performing satisfactorily as a part of the deal.

Can you explain the significance of the McClennan Summation Index reaching negative territory for investors? The McClennan Summation Index (MSI) is a technical indicator that measures the cumulative strength or weakness of the market based on the differences between the closing prices and the opening prices on a daily basis. When the MSI is positive, it suggests that the market is overall trending higher, while a negative MSI indicates that the market is trending lower in a cumulative sense.

For investors, the significance of the MSI reaching negative territory is as follows:

1. **Reversal Signal**: A move into negative territory often signals a potential trend reversal. This could mean that the upward momentum that has been driving the market higher may be losing steam, and there could be a shift towards a more bearish sentiment.

2. **Technical Support**: Historically, when the MSI turns negative, it often coincides with price action that provides solid technical support. This is important because it can help identify key levels where the market might find support and potentially reverse course.

3. **Entry Opportunity**: For those who have been out of the market, a negative MSI can be a signal to reassess and potentially re-enter the market. The indicator can help gauge when it might be a good time to start building a position, as the market could be setting up for a potential rebound.

4. **Risk Management**: Negative MSI can also serve as a risk management tool. If an investor is already in the market, a negative MSI can alert them to the possibility of a trend reversal and prompt them to reassess their risk exposure.

He was a Japanese composer who lived from 1911 to 1988. He was a prolific composer who wrote mostly instrumental and vocal music, and in his career he performed as a violinist, violist, pianist, and vocalist. He was a founding member of the New Japanese Quartet and the composer of their famous Japanese quartets, which were ground-breaking in their use of a Japanese pentatonic scale. Except, of course, that this is not a Japanese quartet. It’s a piano duo, and the first movement is called Bamboo. Although I can’t be sure, I think this piece was written about 1950. The sound is based on the humble bamboo flute. Listen, for example, to the simple, rising and falling, repeated notes that could be played by a child. As I said, this is not a Japanese quartet, but it’s no less an expression of Japanese culture. The opening was written for solo piano and was intended to be played in a meditative state, with the player sitting cross-legged on the floor in a traditional Zen-like position. The second movement is much more memorable and the tempo is much faster. For me, it evokes the way bamboo is blown by the wind. The quick, scherzando, repeated notes in the left hand, are like a breath of air. The second movement is passionate, and I think it might be a portrait of a love that a man has for a woman. The music is bright and lively, and by the end, it’s full of joy. It’s a wonderful, uplifting piece. Half of them entered an IVR environment that simulated a boxing match, in which they played as a boxer – their opponents, played by a computer, did not. The other half watched a video of the same boxing match. Both groups were then asked to play a moral dilemma game in which they were given the chance to cheat. Those who played the virtual game cheated less than those who just watched the video.
The researchers think this is because the students who played the virtual boxing match were more likely to be in a “fighting state of mind” when playing the moral dilemma game. “In the light of your physical involvement, you are going to think of yourself as a fighter and vice versa, not a moral person,” says Hamidifar. “It may decrease your moral sensitivity to behave more self-centredly.” This is different from watching a video of a fight, he says, which may make participants feel afraid rather than angry, and therefore more likely to cheat.
In a second experiment, 28 people of the same age and gender played an IVR game that simulated a violent confrontation between a mugger and a victim, either playing as the attacker, the victim or a bystander. The subjects were then asked to play the moral dilemma game. Participants who played as the victim behaved more morally than those who played as the attacker, and those who played as a bystander behaved even more morally.

The key is to understand that Perry is worried about inflation, and not like, you know, actual inflation. When people say that inflation is low, they usually mean that the Consumer Price Index is rising at a low rate. But Perry is worried about something different, something that’s been a problem for a while and something that can undo the gains of the Fed’s monetary policy. This is called the wage-price spiral. It’s been a long time since we’ve seen it, but when it happens, it can be deadly for the economy.

Here’s how it works. Inflation occurs when spending outpaces production. When the economy is producing at full speed, the natural rate of unemployment, inflation can’t go up too much. But when the economy is producing below its potential, and there’s a lot of slack (unemployment), prices have a chance to go up without causing unemployment to fall. The problem is that if employers start to see that prices are rising, they may try to raise wages too. If employers raise wages, workers will have more purchasing power, and will start to spend more. The higher demand can cause prices to rise more, which causes higher wages, and so on. It’s a vicious cycle, and once it starts, it’s hard to stop.

Perry is worried that the Fed’s loose monetary policy is creating just the sort of inflation that would be the catalyst for this sort of spiral. The problem is that if you’re confident that the Fed will not allow inflation to get out of hand, then you can borrow more or spend more and you don’t have to raise wages to attract workers. In the past, we’ve flown (or carpooled) to these meetings. We remember the excitement of discussing the latest papers, figuring out what to cook for the informal dinner, and of course, of enjoying the famous Beltway conference food. We also remember the flying: the long days and nights, the exhausted bodies, the long stretches of waiting in the uncomfortably warm airport lounges. We have had to agonize over whether to fly, and, in fact, we each had a different decision, and that’s how we and most of the other members of the ASLO community ended up deciding that we would stay home this year.
The conference does matter for our work: we need to know the latest research and make new connections. When we cannot attend in person, we might miss that critical human element that can make science so motivating. Online conferencing has been burgeoning in recent years, and the AGU meeting was already using a conference management platform. So we were able to attend without flying, and we came to D.C. on the train, where we can enjoy the ride and get a little exercise.
Online conferencing is not a panacea. It’s not the same as meeting in person. It’s not easy to convey nuances in tone or body language, and it’s harder to make deep personal connections with people you do not see in person. It’s also hard to start conversations with people you don’t know, and to make yourself known in a crowd. Online meetings, however, can be a substitute or a supplement to in-person meetings. The worldwide spread of internet, smartphones, and social media simply means that we can have more conversations and share our work with our colleagues, friends, and even with people who are not scientists, all around the world. So even without flying to Washington, we can get some of the benefits of the meeting, and we will be able to keep up with the latest developments in our fields.

The Logan Act was passed by the 1st Congress in 1799, and is named after a Mr. John Jay Logan, but his name is on the act for no other reason than that he was a former congressman who sponsored the bill. The Logan Act is a law that prohibits citizens of the US from entering into any diplomatic discussions for the purpose of influencing any foreign government. In this case, the Russian official was the US ambassador to the Russian Federation, but the law was invoked because of an apparently false statement made by Flynn to the Russian diplomat about the US position on sanctions against Russia, which is a very sensitive international issue.
The key part of the Logan Act that is at issue is the following:
“if any citizen of the United States, or person residing within the same, shall, without authority of the United States, directly or indirectly, commence or carry on any correspondence or intercourse with any foreign government or any officer or agent thereof, with intent to influence the measures or conduct of any foreign government or of any officer or agent thereof, in relation to any disputes or differences with the United States, or to defeat the measures of the United States: such person, shall be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than three years, or both.”
The Logan Act is thus an anti-corruption law, a law meant to prevent domestic citizens or residents from mediating foreign diplomacy, and is notably one that applies to non-government people and is not a criminal national security statute. The Logan Act, by being so broadly worded, is centered on the concept of a “foreign agent,” and has long been a source of legal speculation. The meter, on the other hand, is based on a definition that has evolved over time. The original definition of the meter was established in 1791 during the French Revolution. At that time, it was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole along a meridian passing through Paris.

In 1889, the meter was redefined as the distance between two lines on a platinum-iridium bar (the International Prototype Meter) kept at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures in Sèvres, France.

In 1960, the meter was redefined in terms of a specific number of wavelengths of a specific spectral line of krypton-86.

In 1983, the current definition of the meter was adopted: the meter is the length of the path traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.

So, to answer your question, the length of the meter is not based on the foot, but rather on the properties of light and a specific time interval. The U.S. government definition of a foot as 0.3048 meters is simply a conversion factor between the two systems, and the length of the foot is based on the meter in this case, not the other way around. The original meter was defined before the foot in the U.S. system, and the conversion factor was established to facilitate international trade and scientific collaboration. 

In practice, the foot is still used in the United States for many everyday measurements, especially in construction, surveying, and some forms of sports and recreation, while the metric system is used in most other countries for everyday and scientific purposes. However, the definitions of these units are based on different fundamental standards.

Hence a tax on saturated fat could make us healthier. The Danish government’s initial aim was to reduce saturated fat intake by 5 per cent over two years. They predicted that the tax would reduce saturated fat consumption by 10-15 per cent, reduce coronary heart disease by 2.5 per cent and save up to 300 lives a year. A strong case was therefore made for the tax on public health grounds – and I supported it.
But it is important to remember the Danish tax was targeting saturated fat, not all fat. We need some fat in our diet to absorb the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K. It also provides essential fatty acids for cell membranes, and energy for the body. In fact, saturated fat is no more dangerous than fats with a higher polyunsaturated content. In Denmark, as throughout Europe, people are not deficient in saturated fat – it is over-consumption of all fats, and excess calorie intake, that is the problem. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends keeping saturated fat consumption below 10 per cent of total energy intake, and even then only to prevent heart disease, not to lose weight.

The photographer decides which part of the photo should be the sharpest, and the focus tells the camera which part of the photo to display in the sharpest contrast. In all cameras, the focus is achieved by moving the lens in relation to the light-sensing surface, such as the film or digital sensor.
The three main methods of focusing that cameras use are:
- Manual Focus: This is the traditional way of focusing, where the photographer manually moves the lens back and forth to capture the intended subject in the sharpest contrast. - Auto Focus: Auto Focus is the most common form of focusing on a point-and-shoot or DSLR. By using a set of sensors, Auto Focus determines the subject to be captured in the sharpest contrast.

Rogue waves are also known as freak waves, extreme waves and killer waves. They are among the most extreme and unpredictable sea state phenomena that exist. The waves can occur in any ocean, but are often associated with hurricane or tropical cyclone conditions, and are more common in the Southern Ocean near Antarctica. The waves are not to be confused with tsunamis, which are caused by underwater earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.

Bax and his team used a combination of data from the University of Southampton’s Surface Wave Height Estimation and Reporting System (SWHERES) and a state-of-the-art radar system that scans the entire bay.
